text: You have an array cost, where cost of i is the fee for step i. After paying a step's fee, you can climb one or two steps. You may start at index zero or index one. Return the minimum cost to reach the top of the floor.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the fee is paid when you leave a step, and the top is one past the last step. So reaching position i means I climbed up from i minus one or i minus two, paying that source step's cost. Is that right? And are there any constraints on the input size?
Exactly — the top is beyond the last index. There are always at least two steps, and every fee is a small non-negative number.

Got it. Let me run through the example: ten, fifteen, twenty. Start at index one, pay fifteen, climb two, and I reach the top. Cost fifteen. Paying ten then twenty would be thirty, which is worse. So the answer is fifteen.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be greedy — always step to the cheaper of the next two steps. But a locally cheap step can trap you into a costlier path. This problem reminds me of a one-dimensional DP on a staircase: dp of i is the min cost to reach position i. To get to i, I came from i minus one, paying cost of i minus one, or from i minus two, paying cost of i minus two — so I take the min of those two. DP compares both routes at every position.

Here's the plan. One: dp of i is the min cost to reach position i, with n being the top. Two: dp of zero and dp of one are zero — I start free at either one. Three: for i from two to n, take the min of the two routes, and return dp of n. One thing worth flagging — I add the source step's cost, cost of i minus one or cost of i minus two, not cost of i, because you pay when you leave a step. And the answer is dp of n, not dp of n minus one — the top is one past the last step. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code it — and the space-optimized one too.

The table version first: a vector of size n plus one, filled with zeros, so both bases are already free. The loop takes the min of coming from two back plus its cost, and coming from one back plus its cost. Then the constant-space version — only the last two values matter, so I roll prev two and prev one forward. Both compute the same recurrence. One thing worth flagging — I capture cur before shifting, so prev one isn't overwritten before it's used.

Let's dry-run on ten, fifteen, twenty, where the top is position three; expected fifteen. The row that matters is the last one: coming from position two costs ten plus twenty, thirty; coming from position one costs zero plus fifteen. The min is fifteen — start at step one, pay fifteen, climb two to the top. That matches. Bigger case: one, a hundred, one, one, one, a hundred, one, one, a hundred, one gives six — DP routes around the expensive hundreds with two-step jumps. And with just two steps, it returns the cheaper of the two fees. Correct.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear for both. Space is linear for the table, and constant for the rolling version. Oh, one more thing — this is the same one-dimensional DP skeleton as counting ways up a staircase, with the plus replaced by a min over the two routes plus their cost: counting ways versus optimizing cost. If I also needed the actual cheapest path, I'd store a parent pointer per position and backtrack from the top.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You added the source step's cost, not cost of i, and returned dp of n for the top. You explained why greedy fails and DP compares both routes. And you gave the constant-space rolling version with the right assignment order. Good work.
